newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Frenkel says Israel rates will not fall quickly.
newsitem.headline: Frenkel says Israel rates will not fall quickly.

text.p: Israel's inflation rate should be within the official target next year, but interest rates will not come down quickly, Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel told Reuters Financial Television on Monday.
"One should not undertake excessive risks in the direction of too rapid declines in interest rates, because they will come back to haunt you," Frenkel said.

Nevertheless, he said Israel stood a "good chance" of keeping inflation to the government's eight to 10 percent target in 1997. Consumer prices have risen 11.4 percent in the 12 months to September 1996.

Frenkel spoke as the Bank of Israel announced it was cutting short-term rates 0.3 percentage point to an annualised 15.2 percent effective on Thursday. Rates have fallen 1.8 percentage points since August.

The governor said the central bank risked sacrificing its achievements in cutting inflation as well as its credibility if it moved too quickly to ease monetary policy. "We should not rush into all the excitement of stop and go," he said.
He hinted that lower growth might enable him to show more flexibility. "At the present time there is a little slowdown in the economy. This gives us room in restraining monetary policy," he said.
However, he emphasised the importance of government spending cuts, saying the budget package now before Israel's parliament "must be passed".

The government is seeking 4.9 billion shekels in spending cuts for 1997 and officials have indicated they may ask for more once the budget has been passed. "My best judgment (is that) we will probably need to have deeper cuts once the outcome for the year is clear," he said. "I think this view is widely shared."
Frenkel said: "I would not like to be pinned down to a level, but we will need to see deeper cuts in 1997."

He said he would not let monetary policy be swayed by factors other than inflation. Frenkel has come under sharp criticism from business leaders for failing to take into account the damage his restrictive policy has had on the economy, particularly on the shekel's exchange rate.

"I believe the best contribution the Bank of Israel can make to economic performance is to focus on price stability because price stability is the best atmosphere for growth and investment," Frenkel said. "Not because price stability is more important than other objectives, but this is what monetary policy is good at."
He did not express concern about the exchange rate or attribute problems specifically to monetary policy.
"Central bank governors' attitude toward the value of their currency cannot be described in the language of happy or unhappy. The markets should operate with minimal interference," he said.
